# Pañcattaya Sutta (MN 102 (PTS MN ii 228))

**ID:** MN 102 (PTS MN ii 228)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Pañcattaya Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** The Five and Three  
**PTS:** MN ii 228  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pañcattaya Sutta* ("The Five and Three", MN 102; PTS MN ii 228) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya that functions as a middle-length counterpart to the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1), systematically surveying and dismissing an array of speculative views. The text analyzes diverse metaphysical doctrines formulated by recluses and brahmans concerning the post-mortem survival and condition of the self—whether after death the self is percipient, non-percipient, or neither; whether it has form, is formless, or both; and whether it perceives unity, diversity, the limited, or the immeasurable [Polak 2011; Radich 2007]. It also investigates cosmological and pre-existent speculations, such as the thesis that the soul and world were completely happy (*ekanta-sukhī attā ca loko ca*), enumerating sixteen positions accepted on subjective grounds such as faith (*saddhā*) or rational reflection (*diṭṭhi-nijjhāna-kkhanti*) [Jayatilleke 1963]. Declaring all these speculative doctrines to be "conditioned and gross" (*saṅkhata* and *oḷārika*), the Buddha rejects them in favor of liberation detached from conceptual proliferation and rarified modes of perception [Jayatilleke 1963; Stuart 2012; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995; Radich 2007].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: SHT Sutta 24; D 294 མདོ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྔ་གསུམ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། (Pañcatraya-nāma-mahāsūtra)
- Resembling parallels: SF 57

**Sources**

- [Jayatilleke 1963] K.N. Jayatilleke, Early Buddhist Theory of Knowledge (1963) — Analysis of the sixteen theories, subjective grounds of acceptance, and the pre-existence theory ekanta-sukhī attā ca loko ca.
- [Stuart 2012] Daniel Malinowski Stuart, A Less Traveled Path: Meditation and Textual Practice in Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna (2012) — Notes on meditation on rarified forms of perception and the Sanskrit/Tibetan structural parallel Pañcatrayasūtra / lNga gsum pa.
- [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Discussion of the Buddha's repudiation of views of self as 'conditioned and gross'.
- [Fagernes 1992] Proceedings of the 6th Seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (Fagernes, 1992) — Details on the Tibetan title mDo chen po lṅa gsum pa and its Sanskrit reconstruction Pañcatraya.
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation: Ideas about Embodiment in Buddhism from Its Origins to the Fifth Century C.E. (2007) — Description of post-mortem theories of the self and the application of oḷārika/conditioned critique.
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhāna: Towards a Critical Reconstruction of Early Buddhist Soteriology (2011) — Enumeration of the eternalist views regarding post-mortem percipient selfhood.
- [Dhammadinna 2013] Dhammadinna (ed.), Research on the Madhyama-āgama (2013) — Transmission history showing its absence in the Chinese Madhyama-āgama and inclusion in the Mūlasarvāstivādin Dīrghāgama.
